source_text: effectum voluntatis humanae dona caelestia me Bonam - dicis - hominum naturam, quae talis gratiae opitulationem meretur ad capessendam perfectionem adiuvatur
pass_a_gloss: Effectum of-will humanae gifts heavenly me Bonam - you-say - of-human-beings nature, which such of-grace opitulationem meretur to capessendam perfectionem adiuvatur.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: [A person is helped] to attain perfection.
A human being is stirred toward something praiseworthy by the impulses of a noble heart.
Human nature is good, since it deserves the help of such grace.
[I thought he called] the achievement of the human will heavenly gifts.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
In the suum cuique definition gratia is partiality, not saving grace.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
